content.text: Kubernetes doesn't treat your commands as one-off actions. Every object you create records a desired state, and controllers run loops that keep comparing it with what's actually running and fixing the difference. That's why a deleted Pod of a Deployment comes back, a
, and a Pod you create by hand has nobody looking after it.

A team moves its API from virtual machines to Kubernetes and keeps its old runbook. When a Pod misbehaves, the on-call engineer deletes it and then runs the deploy script again "to bring it back". During a traffic spike, someone runs
to eight replicas; an hour later the pipeline's routine
drops it back to three, in the middle of the peak. Meanwhile, Pods nobody touched keep getting new names. The team starts to feel the cluster has a mind of its own.
The belief: Kubernetes is a remote control for containers.
adds a few more, and if a Pod dies, it's your job to start a new one.
It's an honest reading of the tools. The verbs sound like orders, and many developers learned containers with

, where a stopped container stays stopped until someone starts it again. For one kind of object it's even true: a Pod you create directly isn't replaced when it's deleted, as the first tab below shows.

The half-truth: kubectl does send requests to the cluster. But most of them don't start anything. They change a description of what you want, and the actual work is done by loops that never stop running.
Every object is a record of intent
The Kubernetes docs call an object a "record of intent": "once you create the object, the Kubernetes system will constantly work to ensure that the object exists." Most objects have a
, the current state the cluster reports. The docs state the promise plainly: the control plane "continually and actively manages every object's actual state to match the desired state you supplied."
That work is done by controllers. The docs borrow the

from automation, "a non-terminating loop that regulates the state of a system", and use a thermostat as the example: you set the temperature, and it "acts to bring the current state closer to the desired state, by turning equipment on or off." Kubernetes controllers "watch the state of your cluster, then make or request changes where needed."

Controllers rarely touch containers themselves. The Job controller, for example, "does not run any Pods or containers itself. Instead, the Job controller tells the API server to create or remove Pods." The scheduler then assigns each new Pod to a node, and the kubelet on that node "ensures that Pods are running, including their containers." Each piece reacts to what the previous one wrote, and none of them waits for a person.
A Deployment is a chain of loops
Apply a Deployment and several controllers take part. The Deployment controller creates a

from your Pod template and labels it with a hash of that template. The ReplicaSet controller keeps a count: it does its job "by creating and deleting Pods as needed to reach the desired number." It counts every Pod that matches its label selector, not a list of Pods it remembers. When we relabeled one of our three Pods to
, a new Pod appeared within seconds, and the relabeled one kept running with no owner at all.

That's also why the Pods docs say "You'll rarely create individual Pods directly in Kubernetes—even singleton Pods." Pods are disposable; the controller above them is what heals. In the docs' words, "if a Node fails, a controller notices that Pods on that Node have stopped working and creates a replacement Pod."
Commands edit the desired state, and the loop does the rest
Seen this way, each command is an edit.

makes the current state differ from the desired one, so the controller repairs it. Changing the image edits the Pod template, which "has no direct effect on the Pods that already exist", so the Deployment rolls out a new ReplicaSet that replaces them. And
writes your file back as the desired state, replica count included.
We ran this on Docker Desktop's Kubernetes (server v1.34.3, kubectl v1.34.1) in a namespace of our own;
are left out below for space. This file is the whole desired state:

blocks.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.29.8-alpine

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
kubectl run lonely --image=nginx:1.29.8-alpine
# pod/lonely created
kubectl delete pod lonely
# pod "lonely" deleted from readinw-k8s namespace
kubectl get pods
# No resources found in readinw-k8s namespace.

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
kubectl apply -f web.yaml
# deployment.apps/web created
kubectl delete pod web-86c74745c6-gtj47
# pod "web-86c74745c6-gtj47" deleted from readinw-k8s namespace
kubectl get pods
# NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-86c74745c6-4hxtf   1/1     Running   0          1s
# web-86c74745c6-jsvw7   1/1     Running   0          7s
# web-86c74745c6-pb2xz   1/1     Running   0          7s
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
# deployment.apps/web scaled
kubectl get rs
# NAME             DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
# web-86c74745c6   5         5         3       22s
kubectl apply -f web.yaml   # the file still says 3
# deployment.apps/web configured
kubectl get rs
# NAME             DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
# web-86c74745c6   3         3         3       26s

content.text: The bare Pod in the first tab is gone for good: nothing in the cluster wanted it to exist. In the second tab, the deleted Pod already had a replacement, with a new name, by the time
ran. Right after the scale, the ReplicaSet reported 5 desired but only 3 ready, the gap the loop was closing; a few seconds later it was 5 of 5. Then
set the count back to 3, and the controller deleted two Pods.

blocks.title: Take a sick Pod out without killing it

content.text: To debug a misbehaving Pod, change its label instead of deleting it. The ReplicaSet docs describe the trick: "You can remove Pods from a ReplicaSet by changing their labels." The controller starts a replacement, and the old Pod keeps running with its state for you to inspect. Delete it yourself when you're done, because no controller will.

blocks.title: A manual scale lasts until the next apply

The Deployment docs warn that applying a manifest afterwards "overwrites the manual scaling that you previously did", which is the drop back to 3 in the second tab. items.title: Keep the desired state in Git

content.text: Treat the manifest as the truth and change replicas, images and settings there. Anything you change by hand with
is a temporary edit that the next apply can undo.

Controllers are loops that keep moving the current state toward the desired state, without waiting for you.
A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which counts the Pods matching its selector and creates or deletes Pods to match.
A Pod you create by hand has no controller, so nothing replaces it.
